text: A VQE or QAOA program spends time in two completely different places: a classical optimizer loop running on your laptop's CPU, and quantum circuit execution that might be a local simulator call or a network round-trip to a cloud queue. Profiling them as one undifferentiated blob hides which one is actually your bottleneck.

This lesson covers why hybrid programs need profiling split into classical-time and quantum-time categories, using Python's cProfile and simple timing instrumentation to separate the two, why queue wait time on real hardware dwarfs almost everything else, and a worked example identifying where time actually goes in a small VQE loop.

A typical VQE loop builds or binds a circuit, executes it for some shots, computes an expectation value from the counts, and feeds that back to an optimizer. This small amount of timing instrumentation, applied consistently around each of those steps, answers the question that actually matters: of the total wall-clock time for a run, what fraction was the quantum part, and what fraction was ordinary Python work that could be sped up with standard profiling tools.

On a local simulator, quantum execution time is typically comparable to or smaller than classical overhead for small circuits. On real cloud-hardware backends, queue wait — time spent waiting for your job to reach the front of a shared device's queue — regularly dominates total wall-clock time by orders of magnitude, and has nothing to do with your code's efficiency at all. Applying cProfile to a backend-run call against real hardware is close to useless — it will faithfully report that most of the time was spent waiting, without telling you anything actionable.

A twenty-iteration VQE run on a local simulator profiles as roughly 85% classical time and 15% simulator execution time. The same algorithm submitted to real hardware for a final validation run profiles as about 2% classical time, 1% device execution time, and 97% queue wait. These aren't contradictory — they correctly reflect that optimizing the classical loop matters enormously for simulator-based development speed, and matters almost not at all for the cost of a single real-hardware validation run, where the real lever is submitting fewer, larger jobs.

Profiling tells you where time went after a run. Next lesson builds the complementary skill: estimating resource requirements — qubits, depth, shot budget — before submitting, so you can predict and reduce the number of actual hardware submissions before paying any queue-wait cost at all.
